# Diligence Red Flag Analysis

**Company:** Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (RES)\
**Project:** Project Ridgeline\
**Date:** December 2024\
**Prepared for:** Sycamore Capital Partners, LP

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Executive Summary

This memo summarizes the key diligence red flags identified in the review of Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc.’s data room materials. The target presents an attractive regional platform in the environmental services sector, with strong market positioning, regulatory barriers to entry, and consistent revenue growth. However, several material risks require attention, negotiation adjustments, or pre-closing resolution.

### Risk Profile Overview

| Category | Severity | Status |
|:---|----|----|
| Revenue Sustainability (DOE Ceiling) | Critical | Requires pre-closing confirmation |
| Debt Payback on Change of Control | Critical | Requires refinancing coordination |
| Environmental Contamination (Grand Junction) | High | Accrual adequacy validation needed |
| Lease Assignment Defects | High | Landlord consent outstanding |
| Litigation & Claims | Medium-High | Coverage determinations pending |
| Customer Concentration | Medium | Standard for sector; monitor top 10 |
| Labor Relations | Medium | NLRB petition filed; union organizing risk |
| Insurance Coverage Gaps | Medium | Review asbestos/gradual contamination exclusions |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Critical Red Flags

### 1. DOE Contract Revenue Sustainability Risk

**Issue:** The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) IDIQ contract (DE-EM-0005523) generates 19.2% of TTM revenue (\$24.4M of \$127.3M). The \$45M ceiling has 72.7% been consumed in 61.7% of the contract period, with exhaustion projected by April–May 2025—approximately \$12M in FY2025 revenue at risk absent a ceiling increase or new award.

**Implications:** - Potential revenue headwind of 9.5% of current total revenue - Affects valuation multiple and forward projections - Contract requires notice of ownership change to Contracting Officer

**Recommended Action:** - Confirm DOE willingness to increase ceiling or extend contract term prior to signing - Model valuation sensitivity with reduced DOE revenue scenario - Ensure novation/notice requirements are satisfied pre-closing

### 2. Credit Facility Change-of-Control Prepayment Obligation

**Issue:** The High Plains National Bank credit agreement (\$38.7M outstanding) contains a change-of-control provision requiring mandatory prepayment of all obligations within 5 business days of the transaction. A 1% prepayment premium applies to the term loan (\$26.3M), adding ~\$263K to transaction costs.

**Implications:** - Significant cash outlay required at closing (~\$39M+ principal + interest + premium) - Refinancing coordination is mandatory; deal cannot close without payoff - Grand Junction property (with environmental contamination) secures the debt

**Recommended Action:** - Obtain payoff letter from lender with precise closing date amount - Line up replacement financing or ensure buyer cash is sufficient - Consider indemnification for potential late fees/premiums if closing delayed

### 3. Environmental Contamination at Owned Facility (Grand Junction)

**Issue:** The Grand Junction headquarters (owned, appraised at \$6.8M) has documented soil and groundwater contamination from prior operators. The 2019 Phase II ESA estimated remediation costs of \$1.8–\$2.6M; RES has accrued \$2.2M within a total \$3.2M environmental reserve. The 2019 assessment has not been updated, and vapor intrusion testing is recommended but not performed.

**Implications:** - Potential remediation cost overrun beyond current accrual - Groundwater plume migration beyond property boundaries is unconfirmed - Contamination is excluded from Pollution Legal Liability insurance (gradual release exclusion) - May affect lender refinancing, environmental indemnification, or valuation

**Recommended Action:** - Commission updated Phase II ESA with off-site monitoring wells - Require seller to increase environmental escrow or indemnity cap - Validate that accrual covers reasonable worst-case scenario

### 4. Salt Lake City Transfer Station Lease Assignment Defect

**Issue:** The Salt Lake City facility (serving ~\$16M in annual revenue) is leased from Wasatch Industrial Properties, LLC under a 2019 lease. The lease requires landlord consent for assignment/change of control. RES requested consent in April 2022 following the Pinnacle acquisition but has never received written acknowledgment. The Utah hazardous waste permit for this facility remains under Pinnacle’s name.

**Implications:** - Potential default under lease; landlord could assert breach - Additional change-of-control consent needed for Sycamore transaction - Permit transfer remains incomplete - Facility is central to Utah operations and key commercial customers

**Recommended Action:** - Obtain landlord consent to prior assignment and new change of control - Complete permit transfer to RES - Consider escrow holdback for consent uncertainty

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Medium-Severity Red Flags

### 5. Environmental Enforcement Action (CDPHE)

**Issue:** Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment is pursuing an enforcement action (Docket CDPHE-HW-2024-0093) alleging 31 days of unauthorized hazardous waste storage at the Grand Junction facility. Management estimates 12 days of violation and expects a settlement of \$200K–\$450K.

**Status:** Probable penalty exposure; no accrual on balance sheet.

**Recommended Action:** - Include potential penalty in purchase price working capital adjustments - Require indemnification for environmental enforcement matters

### 6. Litigation & Claims Exposure

**Ramirez v. Ridgeline (Personal Injury):** A former employee alleges adverse health effects from exposure at a Wyoming job site. Management estimates \$500K–\$1.5M exposure; coverage determination is pending.

**Wage Claim Threat:** Former asbestos abatement employees claim unpaid overtime (~\$330K total exposure).

**Recommendations:** - Require specific indemnification for these matters - Validate insurance coverage (Ramirez) and assess potential gaps

### 7. Labor Relations (NLRB Petition)

**Issue:** The International Brotherhood of Teamsters filed an election petition (November 2024) covering 62 field technicians at Grand Junction and Casper facilities.

**Implications:** - Potential unionization could increase labor costs and reduce operational flexibility - May impact post-closing retention and operational changes

**Recommended Action:** - Review labor posture and negotiate retention strategies with current management - Consider impact on future labor cost assumptions

### 8. Insurance Coverage Gaps

**Issue:** - **Asbestos Exclusion:** CGL policy excludes asbestos-related claims; RES operated asbestos abatement through September 2023. - **Gradual Contamination Exclusion:** PLL policy excludes gradual releases at owned facilities (notably Grand Junction).

**Implications:** - Long-tail asbestos and groundwater remediation costs may be uninsured

**Recommended Action:** - Review policy exclusions with insurance counsel - Consider tail coverage or additional environmental policies

### 9. Customer Concentration & Assignment Requirements

**Issue:** Top 10 customers account for 67% of revenue. Several contracts (DOE, Intermountain Health, Rocky Mountain Pipeline, Colorado DOT) contain assignment or change-of-control consent provisions.

**Recommended Action:** - Prioritize obtaining consents from material customers (DOE, Intermountain Health) - Model impact of potential customer loss in valuation

### 10. Financial Reporting Quality

**Issue:** - Financial statements are reviewed, not audited - Bank EBITDA (\$18.4M) differs from management EBITDA (\$22.8M) due to excluded add-backs

**Recommended Action:** - Proceed with QoE analysis to validate recurring earnings power - Align covenant calculations with bank EBITDA definition

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Recommendations

| Priority | Action | Responsible Party |
|:---|----|----|
| 1 | Obtain DOE confirmation on ceiling increase or extension | Buyer / Legal |
| 2 | Coordinate debt payoff and refinancing with HPNB | Buyer / Finance |
| 3 | Update Phase II ESA at Grand Junction; commission vapor intrusion assessment | Buyer / Environmental Counsel |
| 4 | Obtain landlord consents for SLC lease assignment | Buyer / Legal |
| 5 | Negotiate specific environmental indemnity and escrow | Buyer / Seller Counsel |
| 6 | Validate insurance coverage and obtain tail if needed | Buyer / Insurance Broker |
| 7 | Obtain customer consents where required | Buyer / Legal |
| 8 | Address NLRB petition before or shortly after closing | Buyer / HR |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Conclusion

RES presents a solid regional platform with defensible market position and consistent growth. However, the critical risks around revenue sustainability, debt refinancing, and environmental liability require proactive management. Addressing these items through pre-closing confirmations, escrow arrangements, and purchase price adjustments will help protect the buyer from post-closing downside.

*This memo is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal or financial advice. Prospective acquirers should conduct their own independent analysis and consult with appropriate advisors.*

# Project Ridgeline — Diligence Red Flag Memorandum

**Proposed Acquisition of 100% of the Stock of Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (the “Company” or “RES”) by Sycamore Capital Partners, LP (“Buyer” or “Sycamore”)**

**To:** Sycamore Capital Partners, LP — Investment Committee and Deal Team

**From:** Transaction Diligence Counsel / Diligence Working Group

**Date:** December 20, 2024

**Re:** Red flag findings from review of the Project Ridgeline data room

**Subject Company:** Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (EIN 84-2135760; CO SOS ID 20091478823)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## I. Executive Summary

This memorandum summarizes the material red flags and cross-document inconsistencies identified in our review of the thirteen (13) documents posted to the Project Ridgeline data room, as supplemented by the executed non-binding Letter of Intent dated October 28, 2024. The proposed transaction is a **100% stock acquisition** of a five-state environmental remediation, hazardous-waste transportation/disposal, emergency-spill-response, and industrial-cleaning platform at an indicative enterprise value of **\$182.0M–\$205.0M (8.0x–9.0x FY2024 Adjusted EBITDA of \$22.8M)**.

Our overall assessment is that the transaction presents a **manageable but higher-than-typical risk profile** for a sponsor buy of this size, concentrated in five areas: (1) the integrity of the earnings base on which the price is based; (2) the imminent exhaustion of the largest customer’s contract ceiling; (3) an uninsured, un-updated environmental liability at the owned flagship facility; (4) a substantial and partly unavoidable change-of-control cost stack; and (5) a set of unresolved lease/permit/labor consents that are not yet satisfied and could delay or condition closing.

**The most significant findings are:**

1.  **The earnings/valuation base does not reconcile.** Adjusted EBITDA is presented as **\$22.8M (CIM)** in one place and **\$23.8M (QofE/CFO schedule)** in another, with an **unexplained \$1.0M gap** the Company acknowledges but has not been able to attribute. Worse, the FY2024 “reported EBITDA” of \$18.4M used as the bridge starting point **equals operating income (EBIT) and omits ~\$7.6M of D&A** shown on the same quality-of-earnings statement (where “EBITDA (Reported)” is \$26.0M). The bank’s covenant EBITDA is yet a third figure (~\$18.4M). The price is being set on a metric that is internally inconsistent. *(Flags F-1, F-2.)*

2.  **The largest customer’s contract is running out of ceiling.** The DOE IDIQ (Contract No. DE-EM-0005523) is the top customer at **\$24.4M / 19.2% of revenue**, but only **\$12.3M of the \$45.0M ceiling remains**, with the ceiling projected to be **exhausted by ~April–May 2025** — while the contract runs to August 2026. The data room itself quantifies a **~\$12.1M FY2025 revenue headwind (~9.5% of total revenue)** absent a ceiling increase. The CIM’s framing of this contract as providing “substantial near-term revenue visibility” is misleading. The contract is also non-assignable and subject to a novation/notification requirement (30-day notice of any ownership change, or termination for default). *(Flags C-1, C-2.)*

3.  **The flagship owned facility carries an uninsured, stale, and potentially under-accrued environmental liability.** The Grand Junction, CO headquarters sits on petroleum- and chlorinated-solvent (PCE/TCE) contamination documented in a **June 2019** Phase II ESA (estimated **\$1.8M–\$2.6M in 2019 dollars**). No updated ESA has been performed in 5+ years despite the ESA’s express instruction to update before any transaction. **The Pollution Legal Liability policy excludes gradual contamination at owned facilities**, and the umbrella does **not** sit over the pollution policy — so this liability is effectively **uninsured**. Additional vapor-intrusion and off-site migration exposure has not been assessed and is expressly carved out of the cost estimate. *(Flags E-1, E-2.)*

4.  **There is a material and partly unavoidable change-of-control cost stack.** Change-of-control severance totals **\$3.775M**, of which **\$2.625M is single-trigger** and payable to the two founder-sellers at closing **regardless of post-closing employment**. The credit facility contains a **mandatory-prepayment-on-change-of-control** with **no waiver mechanism**, plus a **~\$263K term-loan prepayment premium** (total payoff ~\$39.16M–\$39.26M). *(Flags H-1, D-1, D-2.)*

5.  **Several consents and conditions are unsatisfied and could condition or delay closing.** These include the **Salt Lake City lease assignment (unconsented since 2022)** and the **untransferred Salt Lake City hazardous-waste permit** (a facility serving ~\$16.2M of revenue), the **DOE novation**, and the **lease/lender consents** required by the LOI. The LOI also conditions closing on **audited FY2022–FY2024 financials**, which appear unavailable (FY2024 is only “reviewed”). A **union election petition (Teamsters Local 455, 62 field technicians)** filed **November 4, 2024** undercuts the “entirely non-unionized” narrative and implicates credit-agreement notice covenants. *(Flags P-1, E-3, C-2, H-2.)*

**Recommended posture:** proceed, but (a) do not finalize valuation until the QofE reconciles the EBITDA discrepancy (and the EBIT/EBITDA confusion); (b) treat the DOE ceiling, Grand Junction remediation, change-of-control costs, and the Salt Lake City lease/permit as **specific-indemnity / special-escrow items**; (c) require satisfaction of all consents as closing conditions with price protection; and (d) confirm that change-of-control severance is deducted from the purchase price as a Transaction Expense.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## II. Transaction Overview and Deal Terms Reviewed

| **Item** | **LOI / Data Room Term** |
|:---|----|
| Structure | Acquisition of 100% of the issued and outstanding common stock of RES (Stock Purchase Agreement) |
| Sellers | Derek Calloway (32.5%), Jason Calloway (32.5%), Calloway Family Trust (35.0%) |
| Enterprise value | \$182.0M–\$205.0M (8.0x–9.0x FY2024 Adjusted EBITDA of \$22.8M) |
| Adjustments | Net working capital (target TBD), net debt (currently ~\$38.7M), transaction expenses |
| Holdback | 10% of enterprise value (\$18.2M–\$20.5M), 18-month release |
| Indemnity | 0.75% deductible basket; cap = holdback; environmental/tax survival 6 years; general 18 months; fundamental indefinite |
| Timeline | Target signing Feb 14, 2025; target closing Apr 30, 2025 |
| Binding provisions | Exclusivity, confidentiality, expenses, governing law, misc. (Sections 10–15) |
| Buyer advisors | Thornfield & Associates LLP (legal); Bridgewater Forsyth Group (QofE) |

**Data room documents reviewed (13):** Executed LOI; Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM); Litigation & Regulatory Summary; Environmental Permit Summary Schedule; Phase II ESA Executive Summary; Credit Agreement Summary; Corporate Org Chart & Equity Structure; Employment Agreements Summary; Employee Census & Benefits Summary; Insurance Program Summary; Real Property & Lease Schedule; Customer Contract Summary workbook; QofE Data Request Response workbook.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## III. Method and Conventions

- Flags are ranked **High / Medium / Low** on **Severity** (magnitude of value or diligence harm), with a **Likelihood/Imminence** indicator and a **quantified impact** where the data room permits.
- Each flag carries a unique ID (e.g., **F-1**, **E-2**) used consistently in the companion tracker (`red-flag-tracker.xlsx`).
- Category prefixes: **F** Financial/QoE · **C** Customer/Contract · **E** Environmental · **L** Litigation/Regulatory · **D** Debt/Credit · **P** Real Property/Leases · **H** Human Capital/Labor/Benefits · **I** Insurance · **O** Corporate/Organizational · **T** Transaction/LOI · **X** Cross-Document Data Integrity.
- Amounts are U.S. dollars; “TTM” = trailing twelve months ended September 30, 2024.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## IV. Severity Snapshot

| **Category** | **High** | **Medium** | **Low** | **Key theme** |
|:---|----|----|----|----|
| Financial & Quality of Earnings | 3 | 2 | 0 | Unreconciled EBITDA; understated capex; audit gap |
| Customer / Contract | 3 | 2 | 0 | DOE ceiling exhaustion; concentration; consents |
| Environmental | 2 | 3 | 0 | Uninsured GST contamination; permit defects |
| Litigation & Regulatory | 1 | 3 | 1 | CDPHE penalty; Ramirez; wage claim |
| Debt / Credit | 2 | 3 | 0 | CoC mandatory prepayment; management covenant |
| Real Property / Leases | 1 | 3 | 1 | SLC unconsented assignment; expiring leases |
| Human Capital / Labor / Benefits | 3 | 3 | 1 | CoC severance; NLRB petition; 401(k) suspension |
| Insurance | 1 | 2 | 1 | Gradual-pollution & asbestos gaps; tail needed |
| Corporate / Organizational | 0 | 3 | 0 | Dormant Pinnacle; pledged shares |
| Transaction / LOI | 1 | 2 | 0 | Audited-financials condition unmet |
| Cross-Document Data Integrity | 2 | — | — | Numerous numeric/date conflicts |

> GST = Grand Junction site.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## V. Red Flags by Category

### A. Financial & Quality of Earnings

**F-1 (High). Adjusted EBITDA is not reconciled and does not tie across documents.** - The CIM cites **Adjusted EBITDA of \$22.8M**; the CFO’s QofE response schedules produce **Management Adjusted EBITDA of \$23.8M** (a **\$1.0M** difference). The Company states it “intends to reconcile the difference” but “**the specific adjustment category causing the discrepancy has not been identified**.” - The bridge starting point for FY2024 (“Reported EBITDA”) is **\$18.4M**, which is **numerically equal to FY2024 operating income (EBIT)** — not EBITDA. On the same QofE statement, “**EBITDA (Reported)**” is computed as **\$26.0M** (EBIT \$18.4M + D&A \$7.6M). The **~\$7.6M D&A** is therefore either excluded from the “EBITDA” metric or mislabeled. - **Implication:** The single most important valuation input is unreliable. At an 8.0x–9.0x multiple, each \$1M of EBITDA is worth ~\$8M–\$9M of enterprise value; the aggregate unreconciled/definitional spread here is ~\$1.0M–\$7.6M. **Do not finalize price until Bridgewater Forsyth reconciles.**

**F-2 (High). Management’s “adjusted” add-backs are largely non-qualifying and the bank’s covenant metric is materially lower.** - Per the Credit Agreement Summary, the bank’s **Consolidated EBITDA for FY2024 is ~\$18.4M** versus management’s \$22.8M/\$23.8M — i.e., **~\$5.4M of management adjustments do not qualify** (litigation settlement \$1.2M; owner-comp normalization \$0.95M; ERP \$0.65M; Pinnacle integration \$0.8M; asbestos wind-down \$1.8M), with only up to \$0.5M potentially qualifying. - The CIM touts a **1.70x leverage ratio** (using management’s \$22.8M); on the bank’s definition, leverage is **2.10x**. **Implication:** The covenant headroom the CIM portrays does not reflect the contractual calculation; and much of the “adjusted” EBITDA is the very kind of item (owner comp, discontinued ops, one-time) that buyers discount.

**F-3 (High). Maintenance capital expenditure appears understated; the fleet is materially aged.** - Management’s “normalized” maintenance capex is **\$4.0M–\$4.5M/yr**, but FY2024 actual maintenance capex was **\$5.3M**, and the QofE fleet schedule shows **38 of 85 units (44.7%) at or past stated useful life** (average fleet age **8.2 years** vs. **7.0-year** useful life), with a **~\$9.8M past-life replacement backlog** implying **~\$3.3M/yr of catch-up capex** above the current run-rate. - **Implication:** True free cash flow (and therefore supportable leverage/debt capacity and equity value) is lower than the normalized figures imply; a maintenance-capex “true-up” is warranted.

**F-4 (Medium). Historical financial figures are inconsistent across the CIM, the QofE workbook, and the customer workbook.** - FY2022 revenue appears as **\$97.6M (CIM)**, **\$97.8M (QofE P&L)**, and **\$98.2M (customer workbook)**; FY2021 as **\$82.1M / \$82.15M / \$78.9M**; FY2023 as **\$114.8M / \$114.6M / \$115.7M**. Gross-margin histories also differ (CIM shows FY2020 ~33.8%; QofE shows 35.0%).

**F-5 (Medium). Owner-compensation normalization is computed off base salary only and understates the actual premium.** - The \$0.95M add-back reduces the founders’ **base** salaries (\$1.75M) to a \$0.8M market rate. But **actual FY2024 founder total comp was ~\$2.19M** (including bonuses). Bonus “targets” also conflict (Employment Agreements Summary shows 50%/40%/35%; QofE shows 25%/20%). The normalization should be recomputed on a total-comp basis.

**F-6 (High). The litigation-settlement add-back is internally contradictory as to direction and attribution.** - The QofE bridge and the P&L treat the **\$1.2M** “litigation settlement” as a **cost** tied to the **Harper Environmental** matter (“paid Q3 FY2024”). But the Litigation Summary states the \$1.2M is a **settlement receipt** from the separate, resolved **Clearwater Logistics** matter and that **Harper is still pending** (mediation Feb 2025). A cost item that is actually income (or vice-versa) misstates normalized EBITDA and the adjustment’s direction.

**F-7 (High). The audit status of the financials is inconsistent and implicates a closing condition.** - The CIM states the financials “**have not been audited by an independent public accounting firm**” and are “reviewed by … Hansen & Whitfield, CPAs.” The QofE cover states **FY2020–FY2023 audited by Plante Moran PLLC** and **FY2024 (TTM) reviewed (unaudited)**. The two are irreconcilable. - **Implication:** LOI **closing condition 8(i)** requires **audited FY2022–FY2024** financials from an independent firm acceptable to Buyer. If only FY2024 “reviewed” work exists, the condition is unmet; also the lender’s own reporting covenant requires audited annual financials.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### B. Customer Concentration, Contract & Revenue Risk

**C-1 (High). The largest customer’s contract ceiling is nearly exhausted, creating a quantified FY2025 revenue headwind.** - DOE IDIQ DE-EM-0005523: **\$24.4M (19.2% of revenue)** in FY2024, but only **\$12.3M of the \$45.0M ceiling remains**, with **72.7% consumed in 61.7% of the contract term** and **projected ceiling exhaustion ~April–May 2025** — ~16 months before the contract’s stated expiry (Aug 2026). - The workbook quantifies a **~\$12.1M FY2025 headwind (~9.5% of total revenue)** absent a ceiling increase or new award. The CIM presents this contract as providing “substantial near-term revenue visibility,” which is not supported by the data room.

**C-2 (High). The DOE contract is non-assignable and subject to a strict novation/notification regime.** - Per the customer workbook: non-assignable under the **Anti-Assignment Act (41 U.S.C. § 6305)** and **FAR 42.12**; **Clause H-12** requires written notice to the Contracting Officer within **30 calendar days** of any change in ownership or control, and “failure … may be grounds for termination for default.” Novation may be required. This is both a signing/closing condition and a post-closing compliance obligation.

**C-3 (Medium). Customer concentration is elevated and the concentration figures conflict.** - DOE alone is **19.2%**; top-5 **50.4%**; top-10 **67.0%**. Two documents disagree on the **top-20** figure (**89.2%** in the customer workbook vs. **85.0%** in the QoE workbook), and 12 of the top 20 contracts contain **≤60-day termination-for-convenience** rights. The concentration profile is well above the workbook’s own “high risk” benchmark.

**C-4 (High). ~\$16.2M (approx. 12.7%) of revenue is at risk from a single facility’s unresolved lease/permit defects.** - Customers served out of the **Salt Lake City transfer station** (Wasatch Front Petroleum \$6.4M; Silver Creek Mining \$5.8M; Utah DEQ \$4.6M partial; Summit County \$2.9M partial; Bear River Chemical \$1.7M; Uinta Basin \$0.2M) are exposed to the lease-consent and permit-transfer defects described in the Real Property (P-1) and Environmental (E-3) sections.

**C-5 (Medium). Near-term renewal/termination risk on key customers.** - Intermountain Health Systems (\$7.1M) **renewal decision expected February 2025** (concurrent with target signing; the renewal option is not yet exercised). Multiple commercial MSAs auto-renew on short cycles with termination-for-convenience rights (High Plains Energy Partners ~Mar 2025; Powder River ~Jan 2025; Silver Creek ~Jan 2025; etc.).

**C-6 (Medium). The customer dataset appears internally unreliable.** - The customer workbook’s top-20 list and the QofE workbook’s “Revenue by Customer” list are **different customer sets** with different names and amounts (e.g., “Western Slope Municipal Water District \$9.8M” in the former vs. “Western Slope Energy Partners \$8.913M” in the latter; QofE names Rio Tinto, Suncor, Freeport-McMoRan, etc., which do not appear in the CIM). Contract numbers also differ for the same customer (“MSA-2014-CMM-001” vs. “RES-CMM-2014-001”). The reliability of at least one customer schedule is questionable. *(See Section VI.)*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### C. Environmental

**E-1 (High). The owned Grand Junction facility carries significant pre-existing contamination that is effectively uninsured and only partially accrued.** - The **June 2019 Phase II ESA** identified petroleum hydrocarbon (diesel-range organics, BTEX) and chlorinated solvent (PCE/TCE, cis-1,2-DCE) contamination in soil and groundwater, with a remediation cost estimate of **\$1.8M–\$2.6M in 2019 dollars**. The Company’s total environmental accrual is **\$3.2M** across all sites (~\$2.2M allocated to Grand Junction). - **No updated Phase II ESA has been performed since 2019**, despite the ESA’s express recommendation to update “**in connection with any property transaction.**” The estimate is un-inflated (5+ years) and excludes vapor intrusion, off-site remediation, third-party claims, and natural-resource damages. - Critically, the **Pollution Legal Liability (PLL) policy expressly excludes gradual releases at owned/operated facilities**, and the CGL contains a pollution exclusion. The **umbrella does not provide excess over the PLL**. The Grand Junction liability is therefore **uninsured**. The Credit Agreement treats a governmental remediation order \>\$1.0M at any owned property as an **Event of Default** and disclosed the Grand Junction condition to the lender at origination.

**E-2 (Medium). Vapor-intrusion and off-site migration exposure is unassessed.** - The Phase II ESA found soil-gas PCE/TCE above EPA screening levels adjacent to an **occupied** maintenance/warehouse building (potential vapor-intrusion pathway into a daily-occupied structure) and DNAPL potential (PCE/TCE) with no off-site sentinel wells. Both are **expressly excluded** from the cost estimate. Chlorinated-solvent remediation carries the greatest cost uncertainty.

**E-3 (High). The Salt Lake City hazardous-waste permit (UTH-0441) has not been transferred to RES.** - The permit remains in **Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC’s** name; the transfer application has been pending since 2022 (3 years). Under **Utah Admin. Code R315-3**, ownership/control changes require Division approval before becoming effective. RES operates a permitted hazardous-waste transfer station under a prior owner’s permit. The Credit Agreement contains an Event of Default for “**revocation, suspension, or non-renewal of any material permit.**”

**E-4 (Medium). The Casper, WY permit (WY-HW-2019-033) expired November 30, 2024.** - The facility is operating under **timely-renewal provisions**; renewal is expected Q1 2025 but is not guaranteed. Permit-issuance risk, and a potential credit-agreement permit/default issue if renewal stalls.

**E-5 (Medium). The CDPHE enforcement action has un-accrued, disputed penalty exposure and a conflicting factual description.** - Docket **CDPHE-HW-2024-0093** (Notice of Violation dated July 18, 2024). **No accrual** has been recorded. The Company’s position implies a **\$200K–\$450K** settlement (12-day violation); CDPHE asserts a **31-day** violation implying up to **\$1,162,500**. The **CGL has a blanket asbestos exclusion**, and the PLL has a **retroactive date of January 1, 2015**, leaving **2012–2014 work uncovered**; **no tail has been procured**. The Litigation Summary says “no such claims have been asserted to date,” but the QofE Service-Line tab discloses **two open workers’-compensation claims (filed 2021 and 2022) alleging occupational respiratory exposure**. This is a direct conflict and an unreported-to-buyer liability category.

### D. Litigation & Regulatory

**L-1 (Medium-High). The Ramirez personal-injury action is un-accrued and the insurance coverage is disputed.** - *Ramirez v. RES*, D. Wyo. No. 2:24-cv-00187 (filed Aug 12, 2024): a former field technician alleges VOC/heavy-metal exposure at a Sheridan, WY site; **\$4.8M** claimed (including punitive). Management estimates **\$500K–\$1.5M**; **no accrual**. The carrier issued a **reservation-of-rights letter (Sept 19, 2024)**; coverage under the CGL (\$5M) or PLL (\$10M) is **not confirmed**.

**L-2 (Medium). A threatened FLSA/COMPS wage claim adds un-accrued exposure and a classification risk.** - An October 2024 demand from ~8 former asbestos wind-down field technicians alleges ~**\$165K** unpaid overtime plus an equal amount in liquidated damages (**~\$330K** total); management estimates **\$100K–\$200K**; **no accrual**. Management invokes the FLSA motor-carrier exemption, which is itself a litigable classification issue and may signal broader pay-practice exposure.

**L-3 (Medium). The Harper litigation’s status is contradictory.** - The Litigation Summary describes *Calloway v. Harper Environmental Consulting* (Mesa Cty. No. 2023-CV-1847) as **pending** (discovery; mediation Feb 2025), with a \$2.1M affirmative claim and a **\$340K** counterclaim. Yet the QofE bridge/P&L report a **\$1.2M Harper settlement “paid Q3 FY2024.”** Either a settlement occurred (contradicting the Litigation Summary) or the EBITDA add-back is misattributed. (Cross-linked to F-6.)

**L-4 (Low-Medium). OSHA recordkeeping citations contradict the benefits summary.** - The Litigation Summary reports a March 2024 OSHA recordkeeping review at Grand Junction and Casper resulting in **two non-serious citations (\$4,580)**, including failure to timely record three 2023 injuries. The Employee Benefits Summary states “**no OSHA citations issued against the Company in the past three years**.” The under-recording also raises questions about the reported **TRIR of 2.8**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### E. Debt, Credit Agreement & Capital Structure

**D-1 (High). The transaction triggers a mandatory prepayment of all debt, with no waiver path.** - The acquisition is a **Change of Control** under the Credit Agreement (Sycamore acquiring 100%; founders dropping below 51%). Section 2.11(c) requires **prepayment in full within five (5) business days**, **termination of the revolver commitment**, and **cash collateralization of letters of credit at 105%**. There is **no consent/waiver mechanism**; the Borrower must either obtain a payoff letter or refinance. A failure to cure the Change of Control is an **immediate Event of Default**.

**D-2 (Medium). The change-of-control payoff includes a prepayment premium and other costs.** - Term-loan principal prepayment is subject to a **1.00% premium** (≈ **\$263K**) at the target closing window, plus accrued interest and SOFR breakage; the estimated payoff is **~\$39.16M–\$39.26M**.

**D-3 (Medium). A “Change of Management” covenant and a separate Change-of-Control trigger give the lender a claim on CEO continuity.** - Derek Calloway must remain CEO (his departure without a lender-approved successor is an Event of Default), and clause (b) of the Change of Control definition is triggered if he ceases to be CEO absent a successor approved within 90 days. This constrains the Buyer’s post-closing management plan and interacts with the single-trigger severance (H-1).

**D-4 (Medium). Third-party collateral must be released at closing.** - The lender holds a first-priority lien on substantially all assets, including the **patents (Nos. 10,843,117 and 11,205,662)**, the **RidgeTrack platform**, the **Grand Junction real property**, deposit accounts, and **100% of Pinnacle’s membership interests**. Payoff letters and lien/UCC releases are required at closing.

**D-5 (Medium). EBITDA/covenant definition issues (see F-2) mean reported leverage headroom is misleading; no equity-cure rights exist.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### F. Real Property & Leases

**P-1 (High). The Salt Lake City transfer-station lease was never consented to for the 2022 Pinnacle-to-RES assignment, and the proposed deal layers on a further change-of-control event.** - The lease (Wasatch Industrial Properties) **deems any change of control an assignment requiring landlord consent.** The 2022 assignment request was made (April 12, 2022) but **no consent has ever been received**; the landlord sent a new **consent/assignment inquiry in November 2024**. RES occupies and pays rent without formal consent — a **pre-existing potential default** — and the Sycamore stock purchase would add a second, unresolved change-of-control event. The facility supports **~\$16.2M of revenue** (C-4). The LOI makes landlord consents a **closing condition (8(e))**.

**P-2 (Medium). Facility counts/addresses do not reconcile across documents.** - The Company is described as operating “11 facilities,” but the **Real Property & Lease Schedule** (1 owned + 10 leased: including Pueblo, Missoula, Cheyenne) and the **Employee Census** (11 locations incl. Colorado Springs, Pocatello, Helena) identify **different facilities**, and addresses for the Boise, Denver, and Rock Springs locations **differ between the two documents**. This undermines confidence in the facility/permit/headcount population. *(See Section VI.)*

**P-3 (Medium). The Pueblo storage-yard lease expires on the target closing date (April 30, 2025).** - It converts to month-to-month; equipment must be relocated if not renewed (renewal under negotiation). A minor but real closing-date coordination item.

**P-4 (Medium). Multiple landlord consents are required for a change of control; the exact trigger turns on lease-specific language.** - The lease matrix flags consent/notification requirements at Salt Lake City, Ogden, Casper, Billings, Denver, Rock Springs, and Cheyenne. Whether a **stock-level** acquisition triggers each lease’s consent clause must be confirmed lease-by-lease.

**P-5 (Low-Medium). The owned-property appraisal is stale (March 2022, \$6.8M) and no update has been commissioned; contamination may impair value and the asset is collateral for the debt being repaid.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### G. Human Capital, Labor & Benefits

**H-1 (High). Change-of-control severance of \$3.775M, of which \$2.625M is single-trigger and payable at closing.** - Derek and Jason Calloway each receive **\$1,312,500** on a **single trigger** (payable within 30 days of closing **regardless of post-closing employment**); Engel (\$425K), Dillon (\$375K), and Oakes (\$350K) hold **double-trigger** rights (triggered by termination without cause or material diminution within 12 months). The **treatment of these amounts as “Transaction Expenses” is expressly left unaddressed** in the LOI/Data Room. **Implication:** \$2.625M is a certain closing cost (likely a price deduction or leakage); the remaining \$1.15M is a post-closing contingency the Buyer’s own integration/comp decisions can trigger.

**H-2 (High). An NLRB election petition was filed November 4, 2024 — after the CIM was prepared and contradicting it.** - The Employee Benefits Summary (footnote) discloses a **Teamsters Local 455** election petition covering **62 field technicians** at Grand Junction and Casper. The CIM states the workforce is “**entirely non-unionized**” with “positive and productive relations.” This is a **material new development** that (a) contradicts the CIM, (b) implicates the Credit Agreement’s prompt-notice and no-labor-dispute covenants, and (c) represents a genuine integration/operating risk.

**H-3 (Medium). The 401(k) safe-harbor match was suspended for six months (Jan 1–Jun 30, 2023).** - Suspending a **safe-harbor** 401(k) match mid-year may jeopardize safe-harbor status and create an ERISA compliance issue. The Credit Agreement contains a “no ERISA event” representation and treats an ERISA event \>\$500K as an Event of Default.

**H-4 (Medium). Executive compensation and agreement data conflict across documents.** - Bonus-target percentages (50/40/35% per the Employment Agreements Summary vs. 25/20% per the QofE) and the CoC-severance formula (whether it includes bonus) differ. Agreement dates differ for Engel, Dillon, and Oakes between the Employment Agreements Summary, the QofE, and the Org Chart; **Sandra Oakes** is variously described as joining **2018** (Org Chart), **June 2019** (Employment Agreements Summary), and **February 2024** (“newly created position,” Employee Census). These conflicts undermine the reliability of the compensation and labor disclosures.

**H-5 (Medium). Headcount/tenure data conflict and a key “moat” metric is unsupported.** - The CIM states “**over 310** field personnel, **all** of whom hold 40-hour HAZWOPER certifications,” but the Employee Census reports only **148** HAZWOPER-40 holders (and different total/field headcounts). Turnover is described as “below industry averages” in the CIM but “**in line with** industry averages” (~19%) in the Employee Census. The stated operational moat is not corroborated.

**H-6 (Medium). Key-person concentration and retention risk.** - The two founders are integral (the CEO is also the lender’s named “key man”); the LOI conditions closing on executed management/retention agreements (condition 8(g)). Post-closing diminution of the double-trigger executives’ roles would itself trigger severance.

**H-7 (Low). Unused PTO is forfeited on termination in WY, MT, and ID** — state-law exposure (some jurisdictions treat accrued PTO as wages). Accrued PTO liability is ~\$1.4M.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### H. Insurance

**I-1 (High, aggregate). Coverage gaps for the two largest contingent liabilities (gradual pollution and asbestos).** - **Gradual contamination at owned facilities is excluded** from the PLL; the **CGL excludes pollution**; and the **umbrella does not sit over the PLL**. Result: the Grand Junction environmental liability (E-1) is **uninsured**. - The **CGL contains a blanket asbestos exclusion** and **no asbestos tail** was procured; the PLL’s **2015 retroactive date** leaves **2012–2014 asbestos work uncovered** (E-6).

**I-2 (Medium). The claims-made PLL policy is sensitive to the transaction.** - Because the PLL is **claims-made**, the change of control may impair the ability to report claims post-closing and may affect the price/availability of the **extended reporting period (tail = 150% of expiring premium)**. The broker recommends engaging pre-closing to determine whether to buy the tail or bind a new claims-made policy with an appropriate retroactive date.

**I-3 (Low-Medium). Insurance data conflicts on EMR and prior claims.** - **EMR is stated as 0.91** (Insurance Summary, effective Oct 1, 2024) but **0.94** (Employee Census). A **2022 Grand Junction workers’-comp back-injury claim (~\$87K)** appears in the Litigation Summary, but the Insurance Summary’s five-year claims history lists only a **February 2023** back-injury claim for **\$142,300** at the same facility — the two appear to describe the same incident with **different dates and amounts**, and a claim count that may be incomplete.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### I. Corporate / Organizational

**O-1 (Medium). Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC is dormant but undissolved, with live obligations still in its name.** - Pinnacle “has not conducted independent business operations since ~Q3 2022” yet remains a guarantor under the credit facility, holds the **Salt Lake City permit (UTH-0441)**, and remains the named tenant on the **Salt Lake City lease**. The CIM’s depiction of a “**substantially complete**” Pinnacle integration is inconsistent with these open items.

**O-2 (Medium). The Credit Agreement Summary describes RES’s principal office as “Denver, Colorado,”** contrary to every other document (Grand Junction). The **credit-agreement date** is given as **January 17, 2023** in the summary but **September 14, 2021** in the Org Chart. Sloppy, and relevant to confirm the operative loan documents.

**O-3 (Medium). Equity is pledged/encumbered** in connection with the credit facility; the Org Chart itself conflicts with the Credit Summary on the operative date. Clean share transfer and lien releases are needed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### J. Transaction / LOI Issues

**T-1 (High). The LOI closing condition on audited financials appears unmet (see F-7).** Condition 8(i) requires audited FY2022–FY2024 financials from an independent firm acceptable to Buyer; the data room shows FY2024 as **reviewed only**.

**T-2 (Medium). Transaction-expense scope is undefined for the largest closing costs.** - The LOI’s “Transaction Expenses” definition captures professional fees and employer payroll taxes but **does not explicitly address the \$3.775M change-of-control severance**, nor the term-loan prepayment premium. These should be squarely allocated (Seller vs. price deduction) in the SPA.

**T-3 (Medium). Numerous consents are conditions and may drive the timeline.** - Landlord consents (esp. Salt Lake City), DOE novation/notification, lender payoff, and regulatory/third-party consents. The target signing (Feb 14, 2025) and closing (Apr 30, 2025) dates are aggressive given these dependencies. The LOI contains **no MAC out** until the SPA; the target dates are estimates only. ## VIII. Recommended Diligence Follow-Up and Deal Protection

**Valuation & QoE (before price finalization)** 1. Require Bridgewater Forsyth to reconcile the **\$1.0M** EBITDA gap and the **EBIT vs. EBITDA** (\$18.4M vs. \$26.0M) presentation, and to state a single, supportable management-adjusted EBITDA. 2. Rebuild maintenance capex on a **normalized fleet-replacement basis** (accounting for the ~\$9.8M backlog) and re-test free cash flow/leverage capacity. 3. Recompute the **owner-comp normalization** on a total-compensation basis.

**Confirmatory diligence to commission** 4. **Environmental:** updated Phase II/Phase III at Grand Junction (vapor-intrusion and off-site sentinel wells), with a current-dollar remediation estimate; assess prior-owner cost recovery (CERCLA/Brownfields). 5. **Customer:** confirm DOE ceiling-raise/recompete prospects with the Contracting Officer; obtain consents/novation; validate customer schedules and the concentration math. 6. **Permits:** obtain Utah Division of Waste Management status on UTH-0441 and Wyoming DEQ renewal on WY-HW-2019-033. 7. **Labor/insurance:** obtain the NLRB petition file; confirm 401(k) safe-harbor compliance; obtain full loss runs, the PLL policy and tail options, and the Ramirez coverage position. 8. **Real estate:** obtain landlord consents (esp. Salt Lake City) and confirm whether the stock purchase triggers each consent clause.

**Deal protection / SPA terms** 9. Allocate the **\$3.775M change-of-control severance** and the **term-loan prepayment premium** as Transaction Expenses / price deductions. 10. Negotiate **specific indemnities / special escrow** for the **CDPHE matter, Grand Junction remediation (with an updated ESA), asbestos long-tail, and the Salt Lake City lease/permit consent**; carve these out of the basket/cap. 11. Make **all required consents** (landlord, DOE novation, lender payoff) **express closing conditions**, and require **satisfaction of the audited-financials condition** (or a waiver with price adjustment). 12. Include a **CFO-signed closing balance sheet** with tight NWC definitions and a post-closing true-up; address the **DOE ceiling/headwind** through an earn-out or working-capital/EVM mechanism. 13. Size **R&W insurance / escrow** consistent with the environmental and regulatory exposure.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## IX. Conclusion

The target is an attractive, essential-services platform with a genuine permitting moat and diversified demand. However, the data room discloses a **material mismatch between the Company’s promotional narrative and the underlying diligence documents**: the earnings base is unreconciled and internally inconsistent; the largest customer is at the end of its contract ceiling; the owned flagship facility carries an uninsured, stale environmental liability; and a stack of change-of-control costs, unionization risk, and unresolved consents sit between signing and a clean close.

None of these findings is, standing alone, a deal-breaker. But in combination they warrant (i) **price re-testing after QoE reconciliation**, (ii) **specific indemnities / special escrows** for the environmental, regulatory, severance, and Salt Lake City matters, (iii) **all consents as closing conditions**, and (iv) **confirmatory environmental, customer, permit, and labor diligence** before the target signing date. We recommend proceeding on that basis, with the tracker in `red-flag-tracker.xlsx` used as the working issue list.

results.memo:
# 

**Prepared for:** Sycamore Capital Partners, LP (Buyer) — Attn: Elaine Whitford, Managing Partner; Thornfield & Associates LLP (Naomi Vance); Bridgewater Forsyth Group (Catherine Cho)

**Target:** Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc., Colorado C-Corp (EIN 84-2135760), 8750 Industrial Parkway, Grand Junction, CO 81505 — and wholly-owned subsidiary Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC (Utah)

**Proposed terms (LOI 28 Oct 2024):** 100% stock purchase; indicative Enterprise Value \$182–\$205M (8.0–9.0x FY2024 TTM Adjusted EBITDA of \$22.8M); 10% holdback escrow; 18-month general survival / 6-year environmental + tax survival; target signing 14 Feb 2025; target closing 30 Apr 2025

**Basis of review:** This memorandum is based solely on the 13 data-room documents listed in Section 1. No management interviews, site visits, full credit agreement, trust instrument, audited FY2024 statements, tax returns, full 180-page Phase II ESA, underlying leases, permits, or insurance policies were reviewed. All exposures are management-asserted unless otherwise noted and have not been independently verified.

**Use and limitations:** Red-flag analysis only — not a fairness opinion, audit, or legal opinion. Cross-document inconsistencies identified herein mean no single data-room figure should be relied upon without reconciliation. Companion deliverable: `red-flag-tracker.xlsx` (Register + Quantified Summary with formulas + Consents Checklist + Inconsistency Log + DD Request List). Severity and exposure figures tie by RF-ID.

## Table of Contents

1.  Documents Relied Upon and Approach
2.  Executive Summary and Recommended Posture
3.  Financial, Quality-of-Earnings and Valuation (RF-01 – RF-08)
4.  Debt, Liens and Change-of-Control Funding (RF-09 – RF-10)
5.  Environmental Liabilities and Permit Standing (RF-11 – RF-17)
6.  Litigation, Regulatory Enforcement and Labor (RF-18 – RF-23)
7.  Customers, Revenue Durability and Contract Transfer (RF-24 – RF-28)
8.  Real Property and Lease Consent (RF-29 – RF-30)
9.  Human Capital, Executive Arrangements and Benefits (RF-31 – RF-35)
10. Insurance Adequacy and Change-of-Control (RF-36 – RF-38)
11. Corporate Structure, Tax and Transaction Mechanics (RF-39 – RF-41)
12. Cross-Document Inconsistency Log
13. Quantified Exposure and Valuation Sensitivity
14. Recommended Negotiation, Documentation and Closing Posture
15. Further Diligence and 100-Day Plan Requests
16. Appendices

## 1. Documents Relied Upon and Approach

Reviewed (as received, December 2024):

1.  confidential-information-memorandum.docx (CIM, Oct 2024) — TTM 9/30/24 revenue \$127.3M; Adjusted EBITDA \$22.8M; reported EBITDA \$18.4M.
2.  credit-agreement-summary.docx (CFO summary 12 Dec 2024 of HPNB Credit Agreement 17 Jan 2023, as amended 28 Mar 2023).
3.  customer-contract-summary.xlsx (Top 20, Historical Revenue, DOE IDIQ Utilization, Concentration Summary).
4.  qoe-data-request-response.xlsx (Cover, Historical P&L, EBITDA Bridge, Revenue by Customer, Capex Detail, Fleet & Equipment, Executive Comp, Service Line Detail — CFO for Bridgewater Forsyth).
5.  employee-benefits-summary.docx (CFO, 10 Dec 2024; 485 FTEs).
6.  employment-agreements-summary.docx (Greylock Merritt; 5 executives; aggregate CoC severance \$3,775,000).
7.  environmental-permit-schedule.docx (CFO 10 Dec 2024; Grand Junction RCRA COD-098-2761; Utah UTH-0441/0587; Wyoming WY-HW-2019-033; Montana MT-HW-2022-011).
8.  executed-loi.docx (28 Oct 2024; Sycamore Capital Partners, LP).
9.  insurance-program-summary.docx (Frontier Specialty, program year 1 Oct 2024–1 Oct 2025).
10. litigation-regulatory-summary.docx (Greylock Merritt, 12 Dec 2024; ASC 450 assessments).
11. org-chart-equity-structure.docx (CFO 15 Dec 2024; 1,000,000 shares: Derek 32.5% / Jason 32.5% / Calloway Family Trust 35%).
12. phase-ii-esa-executive-summary.docx (Elkhorn EEC-2019-0347, 14 Jun 2019; 12.4-acre Grand Junction site).
13. real-property-lease-schedule.docx (CFO 12 Dec 2024; 1 owned + 10 leased).

Severity scale: **Critical** = could reprice the deal, block closing, or create uncapped/stock-deal successor liability; **High** = material price, escrow, rep or condition issue; **Medium** = manageable via covenant, indemnity or 100-day action; **Low** = housekeeping. Probability follows ASC 450 language where asserted (Probable / Reasonably Possible / Remote), otherwise assessor judgment.

## 2. Executive Summary and Recommended Posture

**Headline: the \$22.8M Adjusted EBITDA on which the \$182–\$205M range is predicated does not survive a red-flag read. Two EBITDA errors alone swing Enterprise Value by about \$18–\$20M, before any allowance for the DOE ceiling cliff, the fleet capex backlog, or unreserved contingencies. The transaction as framed is a 100% stock purchase that imports every environmental, asbestos, permit, lease and employment liability, while the debt, the DOE contract, the Salt Lake City facility (permit + lease), and multiple customer and landlord consents all require pre-closing action on a tight timetable.**

### The five issues that should drive price and structure

**1. Adjusted EBITDA is overstated and internally inconsistent — reprice before signing. \[RF-01, RF-02\] \[Critical\]**

The QoE bridge adds back a **\$1.2M “Harper settlement paid”** in FY2024. The litigation summary says the opposite: the \$1.2M was a **receipt from Clearwater Logistics (paid to RES April 2024)** in a different case, while Harper (2023-CV-1847, RES plaintiff seeking \$2.1M) is still in discovery with only a \$340k counterclaim. If the \$1.2M receipt sits in reported EBITDA, the add-back double-counts income. Separately the bridge computes **Management Adjusted EBITDA of \$23.8M**, a full **\$1.0M above the CIM \$22.8M**, with management noting the difference is “not identified.” Combined, up to **\$2.2M of EBITDA is unsupported — \$17.6–\$19.8M of EV at 8–9x.** The Historical P&L compounds the concern: it shows FY2024 EBITDA of \$26.0M (EBIT \$18.4M + D&A \$7.6M) yet the bridge starts from \$18.4M, i.e., management’s “reported EBITDA” is actually EBIT. Buyer should underwrite to bank EBITDA (about \$18.4M, minimal add-backs) until Bridgewater Forsyth reconciles every dollar, and should require audited FY2022–FY2024 statements (an LOI closing condition not yet satisfied; FY2024 is review-only).

**2. DOE concentration meets a ceiling cliff — about \$12M FY2025 revenue at risk. \[RF-24\] \[Critical\]**

DOE (DE-EM-0005523) is **19.2% of TTM revenue (\$24.4M of \$127.3M)** with **\$32.7M of the \$45M ceiling already consumed (72.7%) about 62% through the period**. At the TTM run rate (about \$2.03M/month) the **remaining \$12.3M lasts about 6 months to April–May 2025** — essentially the target closing date — leaving about 16 unfunded months to Aug 2026. The data-room model itself flags a \*\* ~\$12.1M FY2025 headwind (9.5% of revenue)\*\* absent a ceiling increase or new award. The contract is non-assignable under the Anti-Assignment Act / FAR 42.12 with a Clause H-12 30-day ownership-change notice (failure = termination-for-default grounds), plus termination for convenience. No option periods exist. Underwrite a downside DOE case and tie valuation, earn-out and reps to ceiling relief and Contracting Officer novation.

**3. The Salt Lake City hub sits on an unconsented lease and an untransferred permit — about \$16M of revenue on a defective footprint. \[RF-13, RF-29\] \[Critical\]**

The SLC transfer station (2100 W. North Temple) — serving about \$16.2M of revenue (Wasatch Front \$6.4M, Silver Creek \$5.8M, plus portions of UDEQ, Summit County, Uinta Basin, Bear River) — is still **tenanted by Pinnacle under a lease requiring prior written landlord consent for any assignment or change of control**. Consent requested April 2022 has **never been received** (nearly 3 years of holdover on sufferance; rent acceptance is not consent). The **hazardous-waste permit UTH-0441 is likewise still in Pinnacle’s name**; Utah R315-3 requires Division approval before an ownership/operator change is effective. The proposed 100% stock sale layers a **second change-of-control event** on top of the uncured first.
